implementation_notes: ASP.NET Core ships the whole pattern: AddHealthChecks() registers a health-check service, each IHealthCheck returns a HealthCheckResult with Healthy/Degraded/Unhealthy (plus optional key-value details) and MapHealthChecks("/healthz") exposes the aggregated report, so the hand-written registry, the aggregator and the transport mapping disappear. Tags split the same registry into liveness and readiness endpoints, HealthCheckOptions controls the predicate, the status code mapping and the response body, and RequireAuthorization/RequireHost restrict who may call the endpoint. What remains is deciding which checks belong to liveness and which to readiness and pointing the orchestrator's probes at those paths - and the classic structure is only justified inside the checks themselves, where operations that are expensive or touch shared state need their own timeout and cache.
idiom_name: ASP.NET Core health checks (AddHealthChecks + MapHealthChecks with tags)
pitfalls: The default report writer returns the aggregate status as plain text and the default mapping can still answer 200 for Degraded: set the failure status and the status-code mapping deliberately for the endpoint the orchestrator reads.

Health checks run per request with no timeout of their own: a check that awaits a dependency can outlive the probe deadline, and the orchestrator then reads the endpoint as unreachable rather than unhealthy.

RequireAuthorization (or a health endpoint behind a management port the orchestrator cannot reach) silently turns the probe into a 401/connection-refused, which the platform reports as an unhealthy instance.
